title: AI-generated feedback on writing: insights into efficacy and ENL student preference
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI can serve as an effective alternative to human feedback for student writing and whether students prefer it. The authors focus on a practical educational question: can GPT-4-generated corrective feedback on writing support English as a new language (ENL) learners without harming learning outcomes, and how do students perceive such feedback compared with feedback from a human tutor?

The study reports on two linked investigations conducted at a small liberal arts university in the Asia-Pacific region during Spring 2023. In Study 1, 48 university ENL learners completed six weeks of writing tasks in a quasi-experimental repeated-measures design, with one group receiving feedback from a human tutor and the other receiving individualized feedback generated by GPT-4. Student writing was measured through pre- and posttests rated with an analytic rubric. In Study 2, a different group of 43 ENL learners received both AI and human feedback and completed weekly surveys plus open-ended responses about their preferences.

Results from Study 1 showed no significant difference in writing gains between the AI-feedback group and the human-feedback group, suggesting GPT-4 feedback was not superior but also did not disadvantage learners. Results from Study 2 showed a near-even split in preference between AI and human feedback. Students who preferred human feedback valued face-to-face interaction, engagement, and the ability to ask questions, whereas those who preferred AI feedback emphasized clarity, specificity, and availability. The authors conclude that a blended approach combining human and AI feedback may be most beneficial, especially for language education contexts where efficiency and personalization are important.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s chatbot interface for GPT models, used for generating and interacting with large language model outputs.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as GPT-4 via ChatGPT to generate corrective writing feedback for ENL students’ paragraphs in two studies: one compared AI-generated feedback with human tutor feedback on writing outcomes, and the other compared student preferences for AI versus human feedback.

findings.finding_summary: In Study 1 (n=48 ENL students), AI-generated feedback from GPT-4 did not produce significantly different writing gains than human tutor feedback over six weeks. The mixed 2x2 RM-ANOVA found no significant group x time interaction (F=3.094, p=0.085, partial eta squared=0.063), and no significant between-group effect on posttest scores (F=0.241, p=0.626).
findings.measure: Pretest/posttest academic writing rubric scores (content, coherence, language use, sources and evidence)
findings.effect_size: partial eta squared=0.063 for time x group; partial eta squared=0.005 for group

findings.finding_summary: In Study 2 (n=43 ENL students), preference for AI-generated feedback versus human tutor feedback was approximately evenly split across six weeks. Quantitative survey means were very close for human and AI feedback, and qualitative responses indicated advantages for both modalities (human interaction/engagement versus AI clarity/specificity).
findings.measure: Weekly preference survey items and open-ended responses on feedback satisfaction, clarity, helpfulness, and overall preference

quality_tier_rationale: This is a quasi-experimental mixed-methods study with pre/post comparison and a separate preference survey, but it is not a randomized controlled trial. The design is fairly structured and includes rubric-based scoring and inter-rater reliability, though causal claims are limited by the quasi-experimental setup.
impact_tier_rationale: The main achievement outcome showed no significant difference between AI and human feedback, with only a small interaction effect (partial eta squared=0.063) that was not significant. Student preference was split and therefore does not indicate a strong impact in either direction.
